# A1. How pension designs shape the equilibria {#arg-designs}

Each point of the figure is an economy that has always had the pension design on the horizontal axis, the universal
pension ε, and in the colour, the Bismarckian index θ, read in 2010 under log preferences; every other parameter is
the paper's calibration. A higher universal pension raises the equilibrium tax rate and lowers the savings rate, the
workweek and the savings of informal relative to formal households. A more Bismarckian design lowers the tax rate
and raises the savings rate and the workweek. The black line is the calibrated θ, and its two markers are the
pre-reform ε and the universal level the reform installs. Between them the tax rate rises by more than the reform
raises it on impact in section {{< var p.sec_argentina >}}: here the informal households' savings have always been
those of the universal system, while on impact they still reflect the old one. The difference is close to the
reform's effect a period later, once those savings have adjusted.
